title: Fitting a pull stitch through foam to hold upholstery fabric
subtitle: Use a long upholstery needle and twine to pull the top fabric down through the foam and anchor it to the base, shaping the cushion and preventing the cover from riding up
excerpt: How to fit a pull stitch (through-tie) through foam and fabric to anchor a chair seat cover and give the cushion a defined shape. Covers threading the needle, pulling the stitch through the foam from base to top, and anchoring the thread at both surfaces.
sourceNotes: UK upholstery trade practice. City and Guilds upholstery syllabi (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A vertical stitch that passes a length of twine from the underside of a cushion base, through the foam, and through the face fabric, pulling the fabric slightly into the foam. The stitch is tied at the base and the top is secured by a button or a knot. Used to prevent the top fabric from lifting in the centre of a large seat and to give the seat a slight quilted contour.

A strong, non-stretch flax or nylon twine used for stitching and tying in upholstery. Spring twine is a heavier gauge used for lashing springs; laid cord and mattress twine are finer and used for pull stitches, back stitches, and ties.

When to use a pull stitch

Use pull stitches on large seat cushions (wider than 400 mm) where the foam might dome under load, on wide sofa cushions with a flat top fabric, and wherever a button is to be fitted. A seat that does not need a button but still needs the fabric held flat at the centre benefits from an invisible pull stitch without a button.
Thread the needle and mark the stitch position

Thread a length of upholstery twine through a long curved upholstery needle. Allow at least 600 mm of twine for each pull stitch. Mark the stitch position on the face fabric with chalk. Corresponding marks on the base board (directly below) show where the needle will exit.
Pass the needle through the assembly

From the back of the base board, push the upholstery needle through the board, through the foam, and through the face fabric at the marked position. Pull enough twine through to leave a long tail at the back. Push the needle back through the face fabric 5 mm away from the first exit point, back through the foam, and back through the base board. Pull the twine so the face fabric dimples slightly but does not pucker deeply.

On the back of the base board, pass both ends of the twine through a button shank (if fitting a back button) or knot them over a small square of card or a button to spread the pressure and prevent the twine cutting through the base board. Tie off with a firm non-slip knot. On the face, cover the small pull-through point with a button: push the button's two-hole attachment through the stitch loop before pulling tight. The button sits flush with the face fabric.

attrs.symptom: The face fabric puckers deeply around the stitch point
attrs.cause: The twine was pulled too tight, compressing the foam more than intended.
attrs.fix: Untie and re-pass the stitch, pulling with slightly less tension. A 3-5 mm dimple is correct; a deep hollow means the thread is over-tightened.

attrs.symptom: The twine pulls through the base board on the back face
attrs.cause: Knot or button too small to spread the load, or the base board is thin plywood.
attrs.fix: Tie over a 30 mm square of leather or a large flat button to spread the load over a wider area.
